slides.title: St Patrick's Day
text: Every year on 17 March, Irish people celebrate St Patrick's Day. St Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland. It is a national holiday in the Republic of Ireland and in Northern Ireland.
In Dublin there is a big parade with music, dancers and colourful costumes. People wear green clothes and the shamrock, a small green plant with three leaves.

Millions of Irish people emigrated in the past, so today there are parades in many cities around the world, from New York to Sydney. Some cities even turn their rivers or famous buildings green for the day.

story.title: Under the Swallow
story.subtitle: A letter, a cup and a secret from 1989
story.blurb: On the first day of school, Tiago finds an old letter inside a dictionary. It was posted in Bristol in 1989, it was never opened, and it talks about a stolen cup and a swallow. Somebody at Torre Velha school knows the truth, and somebody really doesn't want Tiago to find it.

characters.name: Tiago Barros
characters.desc: is twelve and in the 7.º ano at a school in Porto. He talks too much, draws comics in every notebook and is never on time.

characters.name: Bia Lopes
characters.desc: is Tiago's best friend since kindergarten. She is organised, sarcastic and wants to be a journalist.

characters.name: Freya Cole
characters.desc: is Tiago's pen pal at Kingsmead Academy in Bristol. She plays the bass guitar and never says anything she doesn't mean.

characters.desc: teaches English at Tiago's school. She wears enormous red glasses and she has a secret.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Dictionary
paragraphs: My name is Tiago Barros, I'm twelve, and I am not a morning person. My mum knows this. My teachers know this. Even our cat knows this, and she doesn't care about anything except tuna.

So on the first day of the 7.º ano, I was running up the hill to school at 8.27 with half a piece of toast in my mouth and one shoe untied. Bia was waiting at the gate. She was holding her new timetable in one hand and her phone in the other, and she was looking at the time in a very dramatic way.
"Three minutes late," she said. "You're improving. Last year it was ten."

Bia is my best friend. We know each other from kindergarten, when she bit my arm because I took her red crayon. Bia is organised, clever and a little bit scary. She wants to be a journalist, and she believes that everybody has a secret. Usually, she's right.

Our school, the Escola Básica da Torre Velha, is old. Really old. The main building has a little tower with a clock that is always seven minutes slow, so technically I'm never late. Inside there are long corridors, blue-and-white tiles on the walls and an old courtyard with an orange tree. This year the workers are building a new library, so half of the school is behind green fences and everything smells of paint and dust.

Our new class director is Professora Helena, who also teaches us English. She's tall, she has short grey hair and she wears enormous red glasses. She seems strict, but when she laughs, she laughs with her whole face.

"This year is special," she said in English, walking between the desks. "Our school is starting a partnership with a school in England, Kingsmead Academy, in Bristol. You're all getting a pen pal there, and in March some of you are visiting them."
Everybody started talking at the same time. Rodrigo asked if English schools have Wi-Fi in the toilets. Professora Helena ignored him.

"It's our first exchange with Kingsmead in a very long time," she said. For a moment she looked out of the window at the old courtyard and didn't say anything. Then she clapped her hands. "Right. Notebooks out, please."

I don't know why, but I think better when I'm drawing. So while Professora Helena was explaining the difference between "I play" and "I'm playing", I was drawing a comic. It was about a superhero called Captain Grammar, who flies over Porto and destroys bad sentences with a giant red pen. Unfortunately, Captain Grammar had short grey hair and enormous red glasses.
"Tiago," said a voice above my head. "What are you doing?"
"I'm... practising the present continuous, teacher."
She picked up my notebook and looked at Captain Grammar for a long time.
"Nice glasses," she said at last. "This week, after lunch, you're helping Senhor Armando in the old library. Every day."
Bia didn't laugh. She just wrote something in her notebook. Later I saw it: "Day 1. Tiago is in trouble. Nothing new."

Senhor Armando is the school caretaker. He started working here before I was born. He knows every key, every pipe and every broken chair in the building. He whistles all day, always the same strange, happy little tune, but nobody knows what song it is. He doesn't talk much. When he sees students running in the corridor, he never shouts. He just looks at them, and they stop.
The old library was dark and cold, and it smelled of old paper and rain. Senhor Armando gave me a pair of gloves and pointed at about a hundred boxes.
"Books in the boxes. Boxes in the van. Understood?"
"Understood."
First, I packed the encyclopaedias. Then I packed the atlases. After that, I started on the dictionaries. That was when it happened.

I was carrying a pile of old English dictionaries to the door when the top one slipped and fell on the floor. It landed open, and something light blue came out from between the pages. It was an envelope, a thin one, with red and blue stripes on the edges. Airmail.

I picked it up. There was a stamp with the face of a young Queen Elizabeth II, and a postmark: BRISTOL, 3 JUL 1989. The address was in neat blue handwriting: "Lena, Escola Básica da Torre Velha, Porto, Portugal."
The envelope was still closed. Somebody wrote this letter thirty-seven years ago, and nobody ever read it.
Suddenly the whistling stopped. Senhor Armando was standing at the door. He was staring at the envelope in my hand, and his face was as white as the paper.
"Give me that," he said quietly.
"It's nothing," I said. "It's just a bookmark." And before my brain could stop me, I put it in my back pocket.

I don't know why I did that. I'm not a liar, usually. Well, not a big one. Senhor Armando looked at me for a long, long moment. Then he turned around and walked out, and he didn't whistle again for the rest of the afternoon.
That evening I showed the envelope to Bia in her kitchen. Her mum was making dinner, so we were whispering.
"We can't open it," Bia said. "It isn't ours. Opening other people's letters is a crime."
"In 1989, maybe."
"It's still a crime, Tiago." But she was already looking for a knife in the drawer. That's Bia. She has rules, and she has curiosity, and the curiosity usually wins.
She opened it very carefully. Inside there was one page, in the same blue handwriting. Bia read it aloud, very slowly.

"Dear Lena, I don't know what they are telling you about me, so I'm writing this. Everybody thinks I took the cup. I didn't. I know who took it, but I promised not to tell, and I always keep my promises. The cup is safe. I hid it under the swallow. The code is the day we met. You know it. Please believe me. Jamie."
Under the name, in small printed letters, there was an address: Kingsmead School, Bristol, England.
Bia and I looked at each other. Kingsmead. The same school as our new pen pals.
"What cup?" I whispered. "What swallow?"
"Tiago," Bia said slowly, "why was Senhor Armando so scared of an old envelope?"
Somewhere in our school there was a swallow, a hidden cup and a secret that was thirty-seven years old. And I had a strange feeling that somebody didn't want us to find it.

chapters.title: Are You a Potato?
paragraphs: For the next two weeks, Bia and I looked at every swallow in the school. There were swallows on Professora Helena's coffee mug, swallows on a poster in the canteen and a ceramic swallow in the headmaster's office. Bia went in with a fake question for the school newspaper and checked under it. Nothing. No cup.
"Maybe Jamie means a real bird," I said. "Maybe the cup is in a nest."
"For thirty-seven years?" said Bia. "Birds aren't banks, Tiago."
Then, on a rainy Tuesday in October, we had our first video call with Kingsmead.

We were sitting in the computer room, two students at each computer, and everybody was nervous. Rodrigo was combing his hair with his fingers. Inês was practising "Nice to meet you" under her breath. I was feeling sick. I talk too much with people I know, and too little with people I don't know, especially in English, especially on camera.
Professora Helena read the names from a list. "Tiago Barros... with Freya Cole."

I clicked on the link. The screen went black, then white, and then a girl appeared. She had red hair in a messy bun, a green school blazer and a striped tie. She was looking at the screen with no expression at all.
"Hi," she said. "Are you a potato?"

I looked at my screen. Somebody from the previous class turned on a funny filter and didn't turn it off. I was a potato, a big brown potato with my eyes and my mouth. Behind me the whole class was laughing, including Professora Helena.
"No," I said, clicking everywhere. "I'm not a potato. I'm Tiago. I'm a person. Normally."
"Shame," said Freya. "I like potatoes."

And that's how I met Freya Cole. She's twelve, like me, and she lives in Bristol, in the south-west of England, with her parents and her little brother. She plays the bass guitar in a band called Weak Tea, and she never says anything she doesn't mean. It's a bit terrifying, but you always know where you are with her.
"So, which year are you in?" I asked.
"Year 8."
"Year 8? But you're twelve. Do you start school at four?"
"Yeah, most people do. We start in Reception when we're four or five, and then we go to Year 1. Secondary school starts in Year 7, when you're eleven. So Year 8 is the same as your... seventh?"
"7.º ano. Yes."
"And do you wear that every day?" I asked, pointing at her tie.
"Every single day. Blazer, tie, black trousers or a skirt, black shoes. Right now I'm wearing my brother's socks, because mine are in the wash. Don't tell anyone."
I told her that most state schools in Portugal don't have a uniform, so we wear what we want. She looked at my hoodie, which has a cartoon octopus on it. "Yeah," she said. "I can see that."

Then she explained her school day. Every morning she goes to her form room for registration, and her form tutor checks that everybody is there. The school is divided into four houses, each with its own colour, and students win points for their house. At lunchtime, some people have school dinners and some people bring a packed lunch from home. School finishes at a quarter past three, and after that there are clubs: drama, chess, coding, rock band.
"And what happens if you fail a year?" I asked.
Freya looked confused. "Fail a year? We don't really repeat years in England. You just move up with your age. But we do big exams called GCSEs when we're sixteen. Everybody's scared of them."
"No repeating?" I said. "I'm moving to England."
I told her about our school too: the tower with the slow clock, the soup at lunch every day, the fifty-minute lessons. When I said that we call our teachers "Professor" or "Professora", she laughed.
"We say Sir or Miss," she said. "Even when we know their names."
"That's weird."
"Calling your teacher Teacher is weird too, potato."
When the call ended, I didn't feel sick anymore. In fact, I was smiling, which was strange, because a girl from Bristol just called me a vegetable.

That evening I sent Freya a message. I didn't plan to tell her about the letter, but I did. I told her everything: the dictionary, the envelope, Jamie, the swallow, the cup. I sent her a photo of the letter. For ten minutes she didn't answer. Then my phone buzzed.
"That's mad. Our library has a box of old school magazines from the 80s. I help in the library on Wednesdays. I can look."
Then another message: "I don't usually do favours for potatoes. But this is interesting."

The next Wednesday, Bia and I were doing our maths homework at my kitchen table when my phone rang. It was a video call from Freya. She was whispering, and behind her I could see shelves of old books.

"Okay, listen," she said. "I was looking through the old magazines when I found this." She held up a thin magazine with a yellow cover: The Kingsmead Voice, Summer 1989. She was turning the pages fast. "There. Can you see?"

It was a short article with the title PORTO EXCHANGE ENDS EARLY. Bia read it aloud: "This year's exchange with our partner school in Porto ended two days early after a serious incident. A valuable silver cup disappeared from the Portuguese school during the farewell party, and one of our Year 8 students was sent home. The school is not planning another exchange with Porto."
"Not planning another exchange," Bia repeated. "Until this year."

"Wait, there's a photo," said Freya. She moved the magazine closer to the camera. It was a black-and-white photo of two kids on a big bridge: a tall boy with a lot of hair and a guitar on his back, and a girl with short dark hair, laughing. Under the photo there was a caption: "Happier times: Jamie Whitfield and his Portuguese pen friend, Helena Matos, on the Clifton Suspension Bridge, April 1989."
Nobody said anything for a few seconds. I could hear the fridge, and my heart.
"Helena Matos," said Bia slowly. "Lena is short for Helena."
"And Professora Helena's surname is Matos," I said. "It's on every test she gives us."

On the screen, Freya wasn't whispering anymore. She was staring at the photo with her mouth open. "That's not the worst part," she said. "Whitfield. Jamie Whitfield. Tiago, Mr Whitfield is my music teacher. And he's walking into the library right now."

chapters.title: First, Then, After That
paragraphs: Freya ended the call immediately. Later she sent a message: "He didn't see anything. I think."
So now we knew two things. First, Jamie was a real person, and today he's a music teacher in Bristol. Second, Lena was Professora Helena.
"We have to tell her," I said.
"Not yet," said Bia. "What do we say? 'Hello, teacher, we opened your letter, sorry, also where's the cup?' No. First we need the facts."

Bia loves facts. On Saturday she came to my house with a huge piece of paper, coloured markers and the face of a detective in a TV series. She stuck it on my bedroom wall and drew a long line across it.
"A timeline," she said. "What happened first, what happened next. Come on."

She wrote while she talked. "First, in April 1989, Lena and the other Portuguese students visited Kingsmead in Bristol. That's the photo on the bridge. Then, in June, the British students came to Porto. After that, there was a farewell party, and the cup disappeared. Next, Jamie was sent home. Finally, in July, Jamie wrote a letter to Lena, and somehow the letter ended up inside a dictionary in our library."
"The important part," said Bia, drawing a big question mark above the word "party", "is who was at that party. And I know somebody who was at this school in 1989."
We said it at the same time. "Senhor Armando."
On Monday we went to find him. Bia had her notebook and her badge from O Relógio, the school newspaper.
Senhor Armando was fixing a radiator in the corridor. He was whistling his strange little tune, but when he saw us, he stopped.
"We're writing an article about the history of the school," said Bia in her most professional voice. "We know there was an exchange with an English school in 1989. Can you tell us about it?"
He didn't look at us. He looked at the radiator. "I was a boy in 1989. Thirteen. I was a student here, and my father was the caretaker."
"So you were at the farewell party?" I asked.

Then he put down his tools. "It was a hot evening in June. Everybody was in the courtyard. The music was playing, the teachers were dancing badly, and the English kids were trying sardines for the first time. Some of them were making faces." He almost smiled. "While everybody was dancing, somebody went into the headmaster's office and took the cup."
"What cup?" asked Bia.

"The Taça de Prata. A silver cup. Our school football team won it in 1955. It wasn't very big, but the headmaster loved it more than his car. When he saw the empty shelf, he went crazy. He stopped the music and asked everybody questions. And somebody saw the English boy, the tall one, coming out of the corridor near the office."
"Jamie," I said, before I could stop myself.
Senhor Armando turned his head very fast. "How do you know his name?"
I opened my mouth and nothing came out. Bia stepped on my foot. "It's in an old school magazine," she said quickly. Which was true. More or less.

"They searched his bag," Senhor Armando continued slowly. "The cup wasn't there. But the next morning they sent him home to England anyway. And that was the end of the exchange." He picked up his tools again. "Now go to class. The bell is ringing."
The bell wasn't ringing. It rang about ten seconds later. That man knows everything.
"His hands were shaking," Bia said in the corridor. "He knows more than he's saying."

For the next few weeks, Bia was busy. Really busy. She was writing the Christmas edition of the newspaper, she was studying for a maths test, and every evening she was messaging Freya. They talked about bands, books and a TV series I never watched. One day I saw them on a video call, laughing about something, and Bia didn't even notice I was in the room. I felt something strange in my stomach. I'm not proud of it, but I was jealous.
"You're spending more time with my pen pal than with me," I said one afternoon.

Bia showed me her phone. She and Freya weren't talking about bands. They were making a list of every swallow in Porto and every tile in our school. Freya was even drawing a plan of our building from photos online.
"We're doing this for you, idiot," Bia said. "Well. For the mystery. But also for you."
I felt like a very stupid potato.

In the end, the answer came from Freya's plan. It was the last day of term before Christmas, and the school was having its Christmas fair. A band of 9.º ano students was playing carols out of tune. I was looking at Freya's plan for the hundredth time when I saw it. In the old courtyard, behind the green fences, she drew a tiny bird on a wall.
"What's this?" I asked her in a message. "An old tile panel in your courtyard," she answered. "It's a swallow, isn't it?"
It was. We never looked there, because the courtyard was closed for the building work. Bia looked at the fence. Then at me.
"Everybody is busy," she said. "Nobody is looking."

First, we waited for the band to start a very loud song. Then we slipped through a gap in the fence. After that, we ran across the courtyard, past the orange tree, to the old wall. And there it was: a big panel of blue-and-white tiles with a river, a boat and, in the bottom corner, a blue swallow flying home.
I touched the swallow tile. It moved.

My hands were shaking. Carefully, I pulled the tile out. Behind it there was a dark hole in the wall, and in the hole there was something square and cold. It was a metal biscuit tin, old and a bit rusty, with a picture of a Scottish castle on the lid. And it was locked with a tiny brass padlock with four little wheels of numbers.
"The code is the day we met," Bia whispered.
Then we heard footsteps on the stones behind us. They were slow, and they were very close.
"Tiago Barros. Beatriz Lopes," said a voice we knew very well. "What exactly are you two doing here?"
We turned around. Professora Helena was standing by the orange tree. But she wasn't looking at us. She was looking at the empty hole in the wall, where the swallow was a minute ago.

chapters.title: The Swallows
paragraphs: There is a moment when your brain stops working completely. Mine stopped behind the orange tree, with a biscuit tin under my jacket and my English teacher two metres away.
Luckily, Bia's brain never stops.
"We're doing a project on azulejos," she said. "For the newspaper. This tile was loose, so we were checking it. For safety."

Professora Helena looked at the hole for a long time. Then she picked up the tile, put it back very gently and pressed it with her hand. "This courtyard is closed," she said in a quiet voice. "It's dangerous. Go back to the fair. Now."
We went. I didn't breathe until we reached the cake stall. When I looked back, she was still standing in front of the wall, alone, with her hand on the swallow.
I spent the Christmas holidays trying codes. 0000. 1234. 1989. My birthday. The date of the last time FC Porto beat Benfica. Nothing. The little brass padlock didn't move.
"There are ten thousand possible codes," said Bia on the phone. "If you try one every five seconds, it'll take you about fourteen hours."
"Fine," I said. "I'm going to do it."
I lasted twenty minutes.

On Christmas Eve we went to my grandparents' flat in Gaia, like every year. We had bacalhau with potatoes and cabbage, and then far too many desserts. After dinner my grandfather saw me with the tin in the living room.
"Where did you get that?" he asked. "We used to have one exactly like it. Your grandmother used to keep her buttons in it."

I didn't tell him the truth, of course. Instead we started talking about the eighties, when he was young and had hair. Grandpa told me that people didn't use to have phones in their pockets. Every Sunday he used to listen to a music programme on the radio and record his favourite songs on cassettes.
"You had to press two buttons at the same time, play and record," he said proudly. "And the DJ always talked over the beginning of the song."

My mum laughed. When she was a teenager, she used to make mixtapes for her friends, with the names of the songs written by hand on the little cardboard cover. "It was the best present," she said. "It took hours. It showed that you really cared about someone."
"Didn't you use to watch TV?" I asked.

"Of course," said Grandpa. "But there were only two channels, and on Saturday afternoons there was nothing good. So your grandmother and I used to go to the cinema on Saturday nights. Big cinemas in the centre of Porto, with red seats and a curtain."
"Two channels?" I said. "What did you do in your free time?"
"We went outside," said Grandma, and everybody looked at me, because I was holding my phone.
Now I watch films on my phone, in bed, at midnight, which my mum says is the reason for my terrible character. But I'm going to make a mixtape one day. I want to see if it really takes hours.
When school started again in January, Freya had news. "I'm doing some research on Mr Whitfield," she said on a video call. "Very professional research."
"You mean you're following him around?"
"I mean I'm observing him."

According to Freya's research, Mr Whitfield is about fifty. He has a long grey ponytail, he drives an old green van and he wears the same black boots every day. He's a good teacher, funny and patient, but he never talks about himself. In his music room there's a cork board, and on the board there's an old photo of a band: four boys with big hair and very serious faces.
"He used to be in a band," said Freya. "He used to have hair like a lion. And guess what the band was called."
"What?"
"The Swallows."
Bia stopped writing. "Like the tile."

"Like the tile," said Freya. "And there's more. Yesterday I asked him, very casually, why the band had that name. He said that a girl he knew when he was young used to tell him that swallows always come back to the same place. In Portugal, she said, swallows mean home. Then he stopped talking and told me to practise my scales."
Something warm and sad moved inside my chest. I thought of Professora Helena, alone in front of the wall, with her hand on the tile.
That same week, Professora Helena gave us some news: the trip to Bristol was confirmed. Twelve students from our class were going, and Bia and I were on the list.
"We're flying on the ninth of March," she said, "and we're coming back on the fifteenth. You're staying with your pen pals' families. Professor Nuno and Professora Carla are going with you."
"And you, teacher?" asked Rodrigo. "Aren't you coming?"
"No," she said, a little too quickly. "I'm not going."

Everybody started making predictions. "It's going to rain every day," said Inês, looking at the weather app on her phone. "I'll eat fish and chips for breakfast, lunch and dinner," said Rodrigo. "You won't," said Bia. "You'll feel sick on the second day."
I didn't make any predictions. I was thinking about the tin, hidden at the back of my wardrobe under my old football boots. I was going to take it to Bristol. I didn't know why yet, but I was sure.
Two days before the trip, at eleven o'clock at night, my phone buzzed. It was Freya. No "hi", no jokes. That's how I knew it was serious.
"Something happened. I was showing Maisie the photo of your tin in the music room, and Mr Whitfield saw it."
"He went completely white. He took my phone and looked at the photo for ages."
"Then he said: Tell your friend to bring it to Bristol. And tell him not to open it. Not without her."

chapters.title: Too Much Ketchup
paragraphs: Bristol smelled of rain and chips.

We landed in the afternoon, under a sky the colour of an old sock. Freya was waiting in the arrivals hall with her mum and a piece of cardboard that said WELCOME, POTATO. Everybody laughed, including me. Sort of.

Freya's family lives in a tall, narrow house with a red door, in a street where all the houses are stuck together. Her mum, Nadia, is a nurse, and her dad, Tom, makes furniture. Her little brother, Alfie, is seven. The first thing he asked me was if Portugal has dinosaurs.

At six o'clock, Nadia shouted, "Dinner's ready!" I looked at my watch. Six o'clock? In Portugal, at six o'clock, we're having a snack. We have dinner at eight, maybe half past eight. But I was hungry, so I didn't complain.

Dinner was shepherd's pie, which is minced lamb with mashed potato on top. There was a vegetarian one for Freya, because she doesn't eat meat. There weren't many vegetables, just a few peas. Alfie put a lot of ketchup on everything. Too much ketchup. A lake of ketchup.
"That's enough, Alfie," said Nadia.
"It isn't enough," said Alfie, and added some more.

After dinner, Tom made tea. He put a little milk in mine without asking. I wanted to say that in Portugal we don't usually put milk in tea, but it was actually quite good, so I said nothing and ate a few biscuits. Then a few more. Freya was counting.
"Eleven," she said. "That's a lot of biscuits for a guest."
On Sunday, Freya said, her dad makes a full English breakfast: eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, toast, mushrooms and tomatoes.
"Every Sunday?"
"Yeah. It's got too much fat for every day. Mum says it's a heart attack on a plate."
In the Kingsmead dining hall there was a salad bar and a hot meal, and on the wall a big poster said: FIVE A DAY! Eat at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day.

Rodrigo didn't read the poster. He ate fish and chips on the first day and said there were too many chips and not enough fish. On the second day, he felt sick. Bia didn't say anything. She just looked at him.
Freya was surprised that I eat soup almost every day. "Soup? Every day? Even in summer?"
"Every day. My grandmother says a meal without soup isn't a meal."
"That's actually healthy," said Freya, a bit annoyed, because she likes to be the healthy one.

But then Nadia asked me how many hours I sleep. I said about seven. She said that people my age need about nine. "Seven isn't enough," she said, in her nurse voice, and I didn't mention the films on my phone at midnight.
On Wednesday we had a geography lesson with Freya's class. The teacher, Mrs Adeyemi, showed us a map.

"A lot of people get this wrong," she said. "The United Kingdom is four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Their capitals are London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. Great Britain is the big island, with England, Scotland and Wales. And the island of Ireland has two parts: Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK, and the Republic of Ireland, which is an independent country. Its capital is Dublin, and they use the euro, like you."
"So England is the UK," said Rodrigo.
Twenty-five British kids shouted "NO!" at the same time.

Freya's gran was born in Cork, in the south of Ireland. "She's coming next week for St Patrick's Day," Freya told me. "She's going to make soda bread and tell everybody that Irish tea is better than English tea."
"Is it?"
"Don't ask that question in this house. It'll start a war."

On Thursday morning, we visited the Clifton Suspension Bridge. It hangs high above a deep valley with a river at the bottom, and it was designed by a famous engineer called Isambard Kingdom Brunel. I stood where Jamie and Lena stood in the old photo.

That afternoon, Mr Whitfield was waiting for us in the music room. He was sitting on a table with a guitar on his knees. He was older than in the photo, obviously, with a grey ponytail and tired blue eyes. When we came in, he stopped playing.
"So you're the potato," he said.
"Freya told you that?"
"Freya tells everybody everything. Except her own secrets." Freya went red. It was the first time I saw her go red.

I took the tin out of my bag and put it on the table. Mr Whitfield didn't touch it. He looked at the Scottish castle on the lid, and he smiled a little sadly. "Shortbread," he said. "My mum gave me that tin as a present for my host family in Porto. I ate all the biscuits on the plane."
"Did you take the cup?" asked Bia. She never wastes time.
"No."
"Do you know who did?"
"Yes."
"Are you going to tell us?"
"No," he said. "I made a promise when I was thirteen. I used to think promises were easy. They aren't."

"Lena and I used to write to each other every week. Long letters, with drawings. I used to send her tapes of my band. After I came home, I wrote to her one last time. She never answered. So I thought she believed them. That I was a thief."
"She never got the letter," I said. "It was inside a dictionary. For thirty-seven years."
He closed his eyes.

"Then she's going to open this," he said at last, and pushed the tin back to me. "Not you, not me. Her. The code is the day we met. She'll remember." He picked up his guitar again. "And tell her something else. I wasn't going to go to Porto in June with the Year 8s. I said I was too busy. I'm not too busy anymore."
On Saturday, at Bristol Airport, everybody was tired and sad. Freya hugged me at security. "Don't open it," she said.
"I won't."
I put my bag on the belt, and it went into the X-ray machine. And it didn't come out. A security officer, a big man with a beard, stopped the belt and looked at his screen. Then he looked at me.
He took out the biscuit tin and held it up. "There's something metal inside this. I need you to open it, please."
I looked at the tin. I looked at the padlock. "I can't," I said. "I don't know the code."

chapters.title: The Eighteenth of April
paragraphs: "You don't know the code," said the security officer slowly, "to your own biscuit tin."
"It isn't exactly my biscuit tin."

That was the wrong answer. The officer called a colleague, and the colleague called another colleague. Professor Nuno came running with his passport in his mouth. Behind me, the queue was growing, and a woman with a baby was looking at me like I was a criminal.

Then Bia stepped forward. She explained everything in perfect English in about thirty seconds: a school history project, an old tin, a lost code, a very important teacher in Porto. I didn't understand half of it, and I was there.
The officer put the tin through the X-ray machine again. He and his colleague looked at the screen for a long time.
"It's a cup," said the colleague, a woman with short blonde hair. "A little trophy. And I think one of the handles is broken."
The officer looked at me. "Did you win something, mate?"
"Not yet," I said.
He laughed and gave me the tin. "Go on, then. Next time, bring biscuits."
On the plane, Bia made a plan. Bia always makes plans on planes. "On Monday we're giving Professora Helena the letter, and we're telling her everything."
"She's going to kill us."
"Maybe. But I think she'll open the tin first."
On Sunday we had lunch at my grandparents' flat. I told them about Bristol: the tall houses, the rain, the tea with milk, dinner at six o'clock.
"Dinner at six?" said Grandma, horrified. "And no soup?"

To compensate, she gave me two big bowls of caldo verde. Then she put too much food on my plate, as always: rice, roast chicken, a lot of potatoes and a little salad. "You're too thin," she said. "You didn't eat enough over there." I ate eleven biscuits in one evening, but I didn't tell her that.
On Monday, after the English lesson, we waited until everybody left the classroom. Then Bia closed the door, and I put the light blue envelope on Professora Helena's desk.
"Teacher, we found this in September," I said. "In the old library. We're sorry we opened it."

She looked at the envelope. She looked at the handwriting. She didn't touch it for about ten seconds. Then she picked it up, took out the letter and read it. She read it again. Then she took off her red glasses and put them on the desk, very carefully, as if they were made of glass. Which they were, of course, but you know what I mean.
"Thirty-seven years," she said.
Nobody spoke. Outside, some boys were playing football and shouting.

"We used to write every week," she said. She wasn't talking to us exactly. She was talking to the window. "In 1989 there was no internet. You waited for the postman. I used to run home from school to check the letterbox. Jamie used to draw little cartoons at the end of his letters." She looked at me. "Like you, Tiago. Maybe that's why I didn't send your notebook to the headmaster."
I didn't know what to say, so for once I said nothing.

"After the party, everybody said he was a thief," she continued. "My parents, the teachers, my friends. I didn't believe them. I waited for a letter all summer. Nothing came. So in September, I started to believe them too." She touched the envelope. "And all the time, it was here, in the library, where I used to study every afternoon."
Then I put the tin on the desk, next to the letter.
"We found it under the swallow," said Bia. "In December. We're sorry about that too."
"The code is the day you met," I said. "Mr Whitfield says you'll remember."
"You met Jamie?"
"He's coming to Porto in June," said Bia. "He told us to tell you. He isn't too busy anymore."

Professora Helena laughed, but her eyes were wet. "The eighteenth of April," she said. "It was raining at Temple Meads station in Bristol, and I didn't have an umbrella. A tall boy with ridiculous hair gave me his. I never gave it back."
"One, eight, zero, four," whispered Bia.
Professora Helena's fingers were shaking. One. Eight. Zero. Four. Click.

She opened the lid. First there was a green-and-white scarf, folded into a square. Inside the scarf there was the cup. It was small, not much bigger than a coffee mug, and dark grey with age, and on one side there were some words: Taça de Prata, 1955. One handle was missing. It was there too, wrapped in an old tissue.
Under the cup there was a cassette in a plastic case. On the cardboard cover, in the same blue handwriting as the letter, somebody wrote: THE SWALLOWS. For Lena. Side B: the truth.
"Side B," said Professora Helena. "The truth."
"So the name is on the tape," said Bia. "The real thief."
"Teacher," I said, "have you got a cassette player?"
She shook her head. "I gave my last one away twenty years ago. I don't think anybody has one anymore."
"We're going to find one," said Bia. "I'll ask my uncle. Somebody will have one."
That was when we heard the noise: a heavy bunch of keys falling on the floor in the corridor. The classroom door was a little open. I don't know how long it was like that.

Bia ran to the door and looked out. I was right behind her. At the end of the corridor, Senhor Armando was walking away fast, almost running. His keys were on the floor in front of our door. He didn't stop, and he didn't come back for them.
The next day, Senhor Armando didn't come to school.

chapters.title: The Saturday Market
paragraphs: After the Easter holidays, Senhor Armando's keys were still on Professora Helena's desk, and Senhor Armando was still absent.
"He's off sick," the school secretary told Bia. "Which is strange. In twenty years, he never missed a single day."

Without him, the school felt different. The clock in the tower stopped completely, nobody fixed the dripping tap in the boys' toilets, and the corridors were too quiet. I didn't realise how much I liked that whistle until it disappeared.
"He was listening at the door," said Bia. "He knows something about that tape."
"Or he's ill," I said. "People get ill."
Bia looked at me as if I was a potato.

Meanwhile, we had another problem: nobody had a cassette player. Bia's uncle had one, but it was in a garage in Viseu, under a boat. My grandfather threw his away in 1995. Online, the cheapest one was forty euros, and it was coming from Germany in three weeks.
"Three weeks!" I said. "We can't wait three weeks!"
"You don't have to," said Professora Helena. "Go to the Vandoma on Saturday. You can find everything there. Things nobody wants anymore, and things everybody wants back."

The Feira da Vandoma is a flea market in Porto, on Saturday mornings, and it's the strangest shop in the city. My dad took us there at nine o'clock and immediately disappeared at a stall with old football shirts. Everywhere there were tables and blankets on the ground covered with things: old phones, lamps, dolls with no arms, keys for doors that don't exist anymore, records, comics, clothes, plates with pictures of saints. People were shouting prices. Somebody was selling a fridge.

Bia loves this place. She buys almost all her clothes second-hand, because she says fast fashion is bad for the planet and also boring. In ten minutes she found a denim jacket from the eighties with patches on the sleeves.
"It's cheaper than a new one, and it's more beautiful," she said. "And nobody else has it. That's the best thing about old clothes."
The seller, a young woman with green hair and a Brazilian accent, said it was the best jacket on her stall. Bia paid six euros.
Then Bia made me try on a shirt. It was orange and purple, with yellow triangles. It was the ugliest shirt in Porto, maybe in Europe.
"It suits you," said Bia. "It's as loud as you are."
I looked in the little mirror. I looked like a packet of crisps. But it was softer than my school hoodie and more comfortable than anything in my wardrobe. I bought it for three euros.
But nobody had a cassette player. "Is there anything with cassettes here?" I asked at every table.
"No, nothing."
"Try somewhere else."
"Nobody uses that anymore, boy."

At last we found a stall full of electronics: radios, old computers, cables and cameras. The man behind it was tall and calm, with some grey in his beard and a woolly hat, and he was repairing a radio with a tiny screwdriver.

For some reason, I decided he was a tourist, or that he didn't speak Portuguese. I don't know why. So I spoke slowly and very loudly in English, like an idiot. "EXCUSE ME. DO. YOU. HAVE. A. CASSETTE. PLAYER?"
The man looked up. "Não precisas de gritar, rapaz," he said, in a perfect Porto accent. That means, "You don't have to shout, boy." Then he added: "Tenho, sim." Yes, I have.
Bia made a noise like a balloon losing air. I wanted the ground to open and swallow me.

His name was Senhor Malam. He was born in Guinea-Bissau, he came to Porto when he was nineteen, and he started selling at the Vandoma twenty-five years ago. He speaks four languages, and he can repair anything with a battery.
"Sorry," I said, in Portuguese this time.
"Everybody makes mistakes," he said. "But you should think before you open your mouth. It's cheaper."

He opened a box under the table and took out three cassette players. The first was a big silver radio, as heavy as a suitcase. The second was smaller and lighter, but it didn't work. The third was a little yellow Walkman with a scratch on the side. It was the oldest of the three, but Senhor Malam said it was the best.
"You have to use new batteries," he said. "And you mustn't play an old tape too many times. Old tapes break easily."
"How much is it?"
"Fifteen euros."
I only had nine euros, because of the shirt. Bia had four. Senhor Malam looked at us, then at the orange and purple shirt in my plastic bag, and sighed.
"Twelve. And I'm giving you the batteries," he said. "But could you please not wear that shirt near my stall?"

On Monday, after school, we sat in Professora Helena's empty classroom: Bia, me and Professora Helena, with the yellow Walkman on the desk and a little speaker connected to it. Freya was watching on Bia's phone from Bristol. Professora Helena put the tape in very carefully, side A first, and pressed play.

First there was a noise like rain. Then somebody started whistling, a strange, happy little tune. A guitar joined in, then some drums. It was a song. A terrible, wonderful song played by four thirteen-year-old boys with big hair, and the chorus was in very bad Portuguese: "Lena, Lena, as andorinhas voltam sempre." The swallows always come back.
Professora Helena put her hand over her mouth. She was laughing and crying at the same time.
Something about that whistled tune was strange. It was familiar, but I didn't have time to think about it, because Professora Helena turned the tape over. Side B.
There was a click, and then a voice. A boy's voice, with a British accent, very close to the microphone.

"Lena. If you're listening to this, you found the tin. I'm sorry about everything. I haven't got much time, the taxi is coming in an hour. I want to tell you who took the cup. I can't say his name, because I promised. But you know him. Everybody knows him. He isn't a bad person, he was just scared, and his dad..."
Suddenly the voice went slow and deep, like a monster in a film. Then there was a horrible sound, a crunching, squeaking sound, and the Walkman stopped.
Professora Helena opened it. A long brown ribbon of tape came out, twisted and shiny, like spaghetti.
"Oh no," she said. "It's eating the tape."

chapters.title: The Boy Who Whistled
paragraphs: If you're under forty, you probably don't know this, but in the eighties everybody used pencils for two things: writing and saving cassettes.

Professora Helena showed us. Very slowly, she took the tape out of the Walkman. Then she put a pencil into one of the two little holes in the cassette and turned it, round and round, until the long brown ribbon went back inside.
"You must turn it gently," she said. "If you turn it too fast, it breaks. And if it breaks, we lose everything."
It took fifteen minutes. Nobody said anything. On Bia's phone, in Bristol, Freya was holding her breath too.
The tape survived, but some of it didn't. When we played side B again, Jamie's voice came back, but some words were missing, like holes in a sock.

"...he was just scared, and his dad... could lose his job... I promised I wouldn't say his name, Lena, and I can't break a promise. But if you really want to know who it is, listen to the beginning of side A again. He taught me that tune. He was always whistling it, every day, even when he was sad."
Then there was a click, and the tape was silent.
Professora Helena turned the cassette over and pressed play. First the noise like rain. Then the whistling: that strange, happy little tune.

And then I knew. I knew that tune. I heard it every day in September while I was packing boxes in the old library. I heard it in the corridors, on the stairs, in the canteen, near every broken radiator in the school. Everybody at Torre Velha knows that tune, and nobody knows its name.
"Senhor Armando," said Bia and I at the same time.
Professora Helena stared at the Walkman. "Armando? Little Armando Pinto? He was in my class. He was the shyest boy in the school. He was always..."
"Whistling," I said.

She sat down slowly. "His father was the caretaker. A very strict man. They lived in the little house next to the school gate. If his son took the headmaster's cup, his father could lose his job. And their home."
"We have to talk to him," said Bia.
"You should leave this to the adults," said Professora Helena. Then she looked at the cup on her desk, and at us, and sighed. "All right. We'll go together. But I'm doing the talking."

There was one problem. Nobody knew where Senhor Armando lived. Professora Helena called him three times, but he didn't answer. At the school office, the secretary said, "I'm sorry, we can't give anybody's address to anyone. It's private."
But in Porto, if you want to find someone, you don't need the internet. You need a grandmother.

"Armando Pinto? Dona Lurdes's son?" said my grandmother on the phone. "Of course I know him. Everybody knows him. Lurdes and I used to buy fish at the same stall at the Bolhão market. They live down by the river, in one of those streets with steps. Ask anybody there."

So on Saturday morning, Professora Helena drove us to the river. We left the car at the top of the hill and walked down a street so narrow that I could touch both sides with my arms. It was steeper than any street in my neighbourhood, and it was made of stairs, not road. There was washing hanging from every window: shirts, sheets, tiny baby socks. An old lady was sitting at her window with a cat. Somewhere a radio was playing, and somebody was grilling fish.
In my building, nobody says hello in the lift. We don't even know the names of the people next door. Here, everybody knew everybody, and everybody wanted to know who we were.
"Armando?" said the old lady at the window. "He fixed my washing machine last winter. He didn't want any money."
"He painted the community centre," said a man outside a tiny café. "All of it. Alone. In August."
"He carries my shopping up the steps every Saturday," said a woman with a walking stick.

A young woman with a baby told us that she came to Porto from Ukraine with her family three years ago. "We didn't know anyone here," she said. "Armando helped us find a flat, and he repaired our windows before the winter. He's the kindest man in this street."
"But he doesn't talk much," said the man at the café. "And this week he isn't talking at all."
His house was the last one, at the bottom of the steps. It was small and yellow, with a blue door, and above the door there were three little ceramic swallows.
Professora Helena knocked. For a long time nothing happened. Then the door opened.
Senhor Armando looked older, and tired, and he wasn't wearing his blue overalls, which made him look like a different person. He looked at us. Then he looked at Professora Helena.
"Hello, Armando," she said.
"Hello, Lena."
He didn't close the door. He stepped back and let us in.

His house was smaller than my flat, but it was the tidiest place I ever saw. There was an old sofa, a television with a lace cloth on top, and a canary in a cage by the window. In an armchair, an old lady was sleeping with a blanket on her knees. "My mother," he said quietly. "She's ninety-one. I look after her."

On the wall, between a calendar and a picture of a saint, there was a photo. Two boys in football shirts, with their arms around each other, laughing at the camera. One was tall, with a lot of hair. The other was small and dark, with his front teeth missing.
Professora Helena took the cup out of her bag and put it on the table, with its broken handle next to it.
Senhor Armando sat down heavily. He stared at the cup for a long time. "You found it," he said. "Under the swallow. I looked everywhere for thirty-seven years. Everywhere except there."
"Armando," said Professora Helena, very softly. "Did you take the cup?"
He looked at his mother, asleep in her chair. He looked at the photo on the wall. Then he looked at us.
"Yes," he said. "I took the cup. And I'm the person who hid your letter, Lena."

chapters.title: The Swallows Come Back
paragraphs: Senhor Armando didn't tell us the rest of the story that day. "I'm going to tell it once," he said, "and I'm going to tell it to the right person. When Jamie is here."
On Monday, the whistling was back in the corridors.

The British students arrived on a hot Friday in June. Porto was ready for São João: there were coloured paper flags across the streets, plastic hammers in every shop, and the whole city smelled of grilled sardines. The new library was finished, the green fences were gone, and the old courtyard was open again, with lights in the orange tree.
Freya was the first off the bus. She was wearing sunglasses and a T-shirt that said I SURVIVED BRISTOL RAIN. "It's thirty degrees," she said, instead of hello. "How do you live like this?"

Behind her came the others. Oliver, Bia's pen pal, who only talks about football. Amira, who wears a headscarf and wanted to know everything about azulejos. And Kai, who uses a wheelchair and plays wheelchair basketball for a Bristol club.
I was worried about Kai. Porto has a lot of hills and a lot of stairs, and our school has some too. On the first morning, Kai saw me making a list of places he couldn't go.
"Relax," he said. "I can't climb stairs, but I can find another way. And I can beat you at basketball. Want to see?"
He could, and he did. Eleven to two.

For the party, my grandmother cooked for half the school. She learnt that Amira doesn't eat pork and that Freya doesn't eat meat, so she made a pot of caldo verde with no chouriço in it, which she says is a crime against Portugal. But she made it anyway, and it was the first pot to finish.
Mr Whitfield was the last one off the bus. He stood at the school gate with his bag, looking up at the tower with the slow clock. And then Professora Helena came out of the door.
Bia grabbed my arm so hard it hurt.
They looked at each other for a long time.
"Hello, Jamie."
"Hello, Lena. Have you still got my umbrella?"
"It's in my car," she said. "I'm keeping it."

That evening, the school had its São João party in the old courtyard. Everyone was there: students, parents, teachers, grandparents, the British group and half of Senhor Armando's street, including the old lady with the cat. There were sardines on bread, caldo verde, and little pots of basil with paper flags and short poems. Everybody was hitting everybody on the head with plastic hammers. It was louder than a football stadium, and much happier.
At ten o'clock, Senhor Armando went to the microphone. He was wearing a white shirt, and his hands were shaking.

"In June 1989, I was thirteen," he began. "Jamie Whitfield was my friend. We didn't speak the same language, but we played football every afternoon. He taught me English songs. I taught him a tune my grandfather used to whistle."

Then he told everybody. On the night of the farewell party, he took the cup from the headmaster's office. It was a joke. The British boys beat our team that afternoon, and he wanted to give them the cup as a prize. But he fell on the stairs, and one handle broke off. He was sitting on the stairs, crying, when Jamie found him.

"My father was the caretaker," he said. "If the headmaster knew, my father could lose his job and our home. Jamie took the cup and said, 'Don't worry. Nobody will know it was you.' Then somebody saw him in the corridor."

Jamie hid the cup that same night, in a shortbread tin, behind the swallow tile. Lena showed him that tile on his first day, because it was loose. The next morning, before his taxi, he recorded his message on side B, ran back to the school, put the tape in the tin and locked it with the padlock from his suitcase. Then he went home, and everybody called him a thief.

"And I said nothing," said Senhor Armando. "Nothing. In July, a letter came from Bristol for Lena. My father always left the school post on our kitchen table, and I saw the stamp. I was sure my name was inside. I couldn't open it, and I couldn't throw it away, so I hid it in the biggest dictionary in the library. Every day I wanted to give it to her. Every day I didn't. In September, when this boy found it," he pointed at me, and everybody turned around, "I felt like I was seeing a ghost."
He looked at Jamie. "You never said my name. Not to anyone. Not even on the tape. You were a better friend than I was."
Everyone was silent. You could hear the sardines on the grill.

Then Jamie walked to the microphone. "Armando," he said, in slow, careful Portuguese, "tu tinhas treze anos. Eu também." You were thirteen. So was I. And he hugged him, a big, long hug, while three hundred people clapped and the old lady with the cat cried into her napkin.

The Taça de Prata went back to the display case in the new library that week. The headmaster wanted to repair the handle, but Senhor Armando said no. "Leave it broken," he said. "It's a better story."

Later that night, Jamie and Professora Helena were sitting on the bench under the orange tree, talking and laughing, and nobody, not even Bia, went near them. Some things are nobody's business. Bia wrote that in her notebook too.

At midnight, Freya, Bia and I watched the fireworks over the Douro from the top of the school tower. Senhor Armando gave us the key. The clock was right for the first time in thirty-seven years, because he finally fixed it.
"So," said Freya, "next year it's your turn to visit us again. Is Bristol going to be as exciting as this?"
"Nothing is as exciting as this," said Bia.
"You don't know that," said Freya. "Our school is older than yours. And the music room has a locked cupboard that nobody can open."

Down in the courtyard, someone was whistling a strange, happy little tune. Then a second person joined in, and then a third. Above the river, between the fireworks, I saw something small and dark flying home in the hot night air. A swallow, maybe. They always come back.

reading.title: The Letter in the Dictionary
text: My name is Tiago Barros, I'm twelve, and I am not a morning person. On the first day of the 7.º ano, I was running up the hill to school at 8.27 with one shoe untied. I was three minutes late. Bia, my best friend, was waiting at the gate. Bia is organised, clever and a little bit scary. She wants to be a journalist, and she believes that everybody has a secret.
Our school is old. It has a little tower with a clock that is always seven minutes slow. This year the workers are building a new library, so half of the school is behind green fences.

Our English teacher, Professora Helena, wears enormous red glasses. That morning, while she was explaining the present continuous, I was drawing a comic about a superhero called Captain Grammar. Unfortunately, Captain Grammar had enormous red glasses too. My punishment: helping Senhor Armando, the school caretaker, in the old library every day after lunch.
Senhor Armando knows every key and every broken chair in the building. He whistles all day, always the same strange little tune, but he doesn't talk much.

First, I packed the encyclopaedias. Then I packed the atlases. After that, I started on the dictionaries. I was carrying a pile of old English dictionaries when the top one fell on the floor. A light blue envelope came out of it. It had a stamp with the face of a young Queen Elizabeth II and a postmark: BRISTOL, 3 JUL 1989. It was addressed to "Lena", at our school. And it was still closed.
Suddenly the whistling stopped. Senhor Armando was standing at the door, as white as the paper. "Give me that," he said quietly.
"It's just a bookmark," I lied, and I put it in my pocket.

That evening, Bia opened it. The letter said: "Dear Lena, everybody thinks I took the cup. I didn't. I know who took it, but I promised not to tell. The cup is safe. I hid it under the swallow. The code is the day we met. Jamie."
Under the name there was an address: Kingsmead School, Bristol. The same school as our new pen pals.

reading.title: Are You a Potato?
text: On a rainy Tuesday in October, Tiago's class had their first video call with Kingsmead Academy in Bristol. Everybody was nervous. Rodrigo was combing his hair with his fingers, and Inês was practising "Nice to meet you".

When Tiago clicked on the link, a girl with red hair appeared. She was wearing a green blazer and a striped tie. "Hi," she said. "Are you a potato?" Somebody from the previous class left a funny filter on, and Tiago was a big brown potato. The whole class was laughing.

That's how Tiago met Freya Cole. She's twelve, she lives in Bristol, in the south-west of England, and she plays the bass guitar. Freya is in Year 8. In England, children usually start school when they are four or five, and secondary school starts in Year 7, at eleven.

Freya wears a uniform every day: a blazer, a tie, black trousers or a skirt, and black shoes. Every morning she goes to her form room for registration. Her school has four houses, and students win points for their house. Some students have school dinners, and others bring a packed lunch. Students in England don't usually repeat a year, but they take big exams called GCSEs at sixteen. And they call their teachers "Sir" or "Miss".

That evening, Tiago told Freya about the letter. A week later, while Tiago and Bia were doing their maths homework, Freya called. She was in the school library. "I was looking through the old magazines when I found this," she whispered.

It was an article from 1989. A silver cup disappeared from the Portuguese school during the farewell party, and a Kingsmead student was sent home. There was also a photo of two kids on the Clifton Suspension Bridge: "Jamie Whitfield and his Portuguese pen friend, Helena Matos, April 1989."
Tiago and Bia looked at each other. Helena Matos was their English teacher! And then Freya said something worse: "Mr Whitfield is my music teacher. And he's walking into the library right now."

reading.title: First, Then, After That
text: Bia loves facts. On Saturday she came to Tiago's house with a huge piece of paper and drew a timeline on his bedroom wall. "First, in April 1989, Lena and the other Portuguese students visited Kingsmead in Bristol. Then, in June, the British students came to Porto. After that, there was a farewell party, and the cup disappeared. Next, Jamie was sent home. Finally, in July, Jamie wrote a letter to Lena."

On Monday they spoke to Senhor Armando. He was a student at the school in 1989, and his father was the caretaker. "It was a hot evening in June," he said. "The music was playing, the teachers were dancing badly, and the English kids were trying sardines for the first time. While everybody was dancing, somebody went into the headmaster's office and took the cup."

It was a small silver cup. The school football team won it in 1955. Somebody saw Jamie near the office, so they searched his bag. The cup wasn't there, but the next morning they sent him home anyway. While Senhor Armando was talking, his hands were shaking.

For the next few weeks, Bia was very busy, and she was messaging Freya every evening. Tiago felt jealous. "You're spending more time with my pen pal than with me," he said. But Bia showed him her phone. She and Freya were making a list of every swallow in Porto and every tile in the school. They were doing it for him.

On the last day of term, during the Christmas fair, Tiago was looking at Freya's plan of the school when he saw a tiny bird: a swallow on an old tile panel in the courtyard. The courtyard was closed for building work. First, Tiago and Bia waited for a loud song. Then they slipped through a gap in the fence. After that, they ran to the old wall. Tiago touched the swallow tile, and it moved. Behind it there was a rusty biscuit tin, locked with a small padlock with four numbers.
Then they heard footsteps. "What exactly are you two doing here?" It was Professora Helena. But she wasn't looking at them. She was looking at the hole in the wall.

reading.title: The Swallows
text: Bia's brain never stops. When Professora Helena found them in the courtyard, Bia said, "We're doing a project on azulejos. This tile was loose, so we were checking it." The teacher put the tile back and sent them away. When Tiago looked back, she was standing in front of the wall, alone, with her hand on the swallow.

Tiago spent the Christmas holidays trying codes: 0000, 1234, 1989, his birthday. Nothing worked. "There are ten thousand possible codes," said Bia. "If you try one every five seconds, it'll take about fourteen hours." Tiago lasted twenty minutes.

On Christmas Eve, at his grandparents' flat, his grandfather saw the tin. "We used to have one exactly like it," he said. "Your grandmother used to keep her buttons in it." Then they talked about the eighties. People didn't use to have phones in their pockets. Every Sunday Grandpa used to record his favourite songs from the radio on cassettes. Tiago's mum used to make mixtapes for her friends. "Didn't you use to watch TV?" Tiago asked. "There were only two channels," said Grandpa. "So we used to go to the cinema on Saturday nights."

In January, Freya started some "very professional research" on Mr Whitfield. He is about fifty, he has a long grey ponytail and he drives an old green van. In his music room there is an old photo of a band. "He used to be in a band," Freya said. "He used to have hair like a lion. And the band was called The Swallows." Mr Whitfield told her that a girl he knew used to say that swallows always come back to the same place. In Portugal, swallows mean home.
Then the trip to Bristol was confirmed. "We're flying on the ninth of March," said Professora Helena. But she wasn't going. Tiago decided to take the tin with him.

Two days before the trip, Freya sent a message: "Mr Whitfield saw the photo of your tin on my phone. He went completely white. He said: Tell your friend to bring it to Bristol. And tell him not to open it. Not without her."

reading.title: Too Much Ketchup
text: Bristol smelled of rain and chips. Freya was waiting at the airport with a piece of cardboard that said WELCOME, POTATO.

Freya's family lives in a tall, narrow house with a red door. At six o'clock her mum, Nadia, shouted, "Dinner's ready!" Tiago was surprised. In Portugal, people usually have dinner at eight or later. Dinner was shepherd's pie, minced lamb with mashed potato on top, and there was a vegetarian one for Freya. There weren't many vegetables, just a few peas. Freya's little brother, Alfie, put too much ketchup on everything. "That's enough, Alfie," said Nadia. After dinner, Tiago had tea with a little milk and ate a lot of biscuits. Eleven, in fact. Freya counted.
On Sundays, Freya's dad makes a full English breakfast: eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, toast, mushrooms and tomatoes. "It's got too much fat for every day," Freya said.

At school, a big poster said: FIVE A DAY! Eat at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day. Rodrigo ate fish and chips and said there were too many chips and not enough fish. Freya was surprised that Tiago eats soup almost every day. "That's actually healthy," she said. But Tiago only sleeps about seven hours a night, and Nadia, a nurse, said that isn't enough.

In a geography lesson, Mrs Adeyemi explained that the United Kingdom is four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with the capitals London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. The island of Ireland has two parts: Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK, and the Republic of Ireland, an independent country. Its capital is Dublin, and it uses the euro. Freya's gran was born in Cork, in Ireland, and she says Irish tea is better than English tea.

On Thursday they visited the Clifton Suspension Bridge, designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel. Then Mr Whitfield told them his story. "I didn't take the cup," he said. "I know who did, but I made a promise." He gave the tin back. "Lena has to open it. The code is the day we met."

At the airport, Tiago's bag went into the X-ray machine and didn't come out. "There's something metal inside this tin," said a security officer. "Open it, please." "I can't," said Tiago. "I don't know the code."

reading.title: The Eighteenth of April
text: At Bristol Airport, the security officer put the tin through the X-ray machine again. "It's a cup," said his colleague. "A little trophy. One of the handles is broken." The officer laughed. "Did you win something, mate?" "Not yet," said Tiago.

On the plane, Bia made a plan. "On Monday we're going to give Professora Helena the letter, and we're going to tell her everything." "She's going to kill us," said Tiago. "Maybe. But I think she'll open the tin first."

On Monday, after the English lesson, they put the light blue envelope on the teacher's desk. Professora Helena read the letter twice. Then she took off her red glasses. "Thirty-seven years," she said.

"We used to write every week," she said, looking at the window. "There was no internet. I used to run home from school to check the letterbox. Jamie used to draw little cartoons at the end of his letters. After the party, everybody said he was a thief. I waited for a letter all summer. Nothing came. So in September, I started to believe them too."
Then Tiago put the tin on the desk. "The code is the day you met. Mr Whitfield says you'll remember. And he's coming to Porto in June."

Professora Helena laughed, but her eyes were wet. "The eighteenth of April. It was raining at Temple Meads station in Bristol, and a tall boy with ridiculous hair gave me his umbrella. I never gave it back."
One. Eight. Zero. Four. Click.

Inside the tin there was a green-and-white scarf, and inside the scarf there was the cup: small, dark grey, with the words Taça de Prata, 1955. One handle was broken. Under the cup there was a cassette. On the cover someone wrote: THE SWALLOWS. For Lena. Side B: the truth.
"Have you got a cassette player, teacher?" asked Tiago. "No. I don't think anybody has one anymore." "We're going to find one," said Bia. "Somebody will have one."

Then they heard a noise: a bunch of keys falling on the floor in the corridor. Senhor Armando was walking away fast, almost running. He didn't come back for his keys. The next day, he didn't come to school.

reading.title: The Saturday Market
text: After the Easter holidays, Senhor Armando was still absent. "He's off sick," the school secretary said. "In twenty years, he never missed a single day."

Tiago and Bia had another problem: nobody had a cassette player. Online, the cheapest one was forty euros, and it was coming from Germany in three weeks. "Go to the Vandoma on Saturday," said Professora Helena. "You can find everything there."

The Feira da Vandoma is a flea market in Porto, on Saturday mornings. There were tables and blankets on the ground covered with old phones, lamps, records, comics, clothes and keys. Somebody was even selling a fridge.

Bia buys almost all her clothes second-hand, because she says fast fashion is bad for the planet. She found a denim jacket from the eighties for six euros. "It's cheaper than a new one, and it's more beautiful," she said. "And nobody else has it." Then she made Tiago try on an orange and purple shirt with yellow triangles. It was the ugliest shirt in Porto. "It's as loud as you are," said Bia. But it was more comfortable than his school hoodie, so Tiago bought it for three euros.

At last they found a stall full of electronics. The man behind it was repairing a radio. For some reason, Tiago decided that he didn't speak Portuguese, so he shouted in English: "DO. YOU. HAVE. A. CASSETTE. PLAYER?" The man looked up. "Não precisas de gritar, rapaz," he said, in a perfect Porto accent. You don't have to shout, boy.

His name was Senhor Malam. He was born in Guinea-Bissau and came to Porto when he was nineteen. He speaks four languages and can repair anything with a battery. "Everybody makes mistakes," he said. "But you should think before you open your mouth."

He showed them three cassette players. The first was a big silver radio, as heavy as a suitcase. The second was smaller and lighter, but it didn't work. The third, a yellow Walkman, was the oldest, but it was the best. They paid twelve euros.

On Monday they listened to the tape with Professora Helena. Side A was a song by The Swallows. Side B was Jamie's voice: "I want to tell you who took the cup. He isn't a bad person, he was just scared, and his dad..." Then the Walkman made a horrible noise. It was eating the tape.

reading.title: The Boy Who Whistled
text: In the eighties, everybody knew how to save a cassette with a pencil. Professora Helena put a pencil into one of the little holes and turned it, round and round, until the tape went back inside. "You must turn it gently," she said. "If you turn it too fast, it breaks."

The tape survived, but some words were missing. "...his dad... could lose his job... I promised I wouldn't say his name. But if you want to know who it is, listen to the beginning of side A again. He taught me that tune. He was always whistling it."

They played side A. First a noise like rain, then the whistling: a strange, happy little tune. Tiago knew that tune. Everybody at school knew it. "Senhor Armando," said Tiago and Bia at the same time.
"Little Armando Pinto?" said Professora Helena. "He was in my class. His father was the caretaker, a very strict man. If his son took the headmaster's cup, he could lose his job."

Nobody knew where Senhor Armando lived. The school secretary said, "We can't give anybody's address to anyone." But Tiago's grandmother knew his mother. "They live down by the river, in one of those streets with steps. Ask anybody there."

On Saturday, Professora Helena drove them to the river. The street was narrower and steeper than any street in Tiago's neighbourhood, with washing hanging from every window. In Tiago's building, nobody says hello in the lift. Here, everybody knew everybody.

"He fixed my washing machine," said an old lady. "He painted the community centre," said a man at the café. A young woman from Ukraine said Armando helped her family find a flat. "He's the kindest man in this street. But he doesn't talk much."

His house was small and yellow, with three ceramic swallows above the blue door. Senhor Armando opened it. "Hello, Lena," he said. His house was smaller than Tiago's flat, but it was very tidy. His old mother was sleeping in an armchair. "She's ninety-one. I look after her." On the wall there was a photo of two boys in football shirts: Jamie and a young Armando.
Professora Helena put the cup on the table. "Armando, did you take the cup?"
"Yes," he said. "I took the cup. And I'm the person who hid your letter, Lena."

reading.title: The Swallows Come Back
text: The British students arrived on a hot Friday in June, when Porto was getting ready for São João. Freya was the first off the bus. "It's thirty degrees," she said. "How do you live like this?"

With her came Oliver, who only talks about football, Amira, who wears a headscarf and loves azulejos, and Kai, who uses a wheelchair and plays wheelchair basketball. Tiago was worried about all the hills and stairs in Porto, but Kai said, "Relax. I can't climb stairs, but I can find another way. And I can beat you at basketball." He did: eleven to two.
Amira doesn't eat pork and Freya doesn't eat meat, so Tiago's grandmother made caldo verde without chouriço. She says it's a crime against Portugal, but it was the first pot to finish.
Then Mr Whitfield got off the bus, and Professora Helena came out of the school. "Hello, Jamie." "Hello, Lena. Have you still got my umbrella?" "It's in my car. I'm keeping it."

That evening, everybody came to the São João party in the old courtyard. At ten o'clock, Senhor Armando went to the microphone and told the whole story. In 1989 he was thirteen, and Jamie was his friend. He took the cup as a joke, but he fell on the stairs and broke a handle. Jamie found him crying and said, "Don't worry. Nobody will know it was you." Jamie hid the cup behind the swallow tile, and the next morning he was sent home. Later, when the letter arrived from Bristol, Armando was scared that his name was inside, so he hid it in a dictionary.
"You never said my name," Armando told Jamie. "Not to anyone. You were a better friend than I was."
Jamie answered in Portuguese: "Tu tinhas treze anos. Eu também." You were thirteen. So was I. Then he hugged him, and everybody clapped.
The cup went back to the school library. "Leave the handle broken," said Armando. "It's a better story."

At midnight, Tiago, Bia and Freya watched the fireworks over the Douro from the top of the school tower. "Next year it's your turn to visit us," said Freya. "Our music room has a locked cupboard that nobody can open." Down in the courtyard, someone was whistling a strange, happy little tune. Swallows always come back.

sebenta.title: Present Simple
sebenta.html:
Form

AffirmativeNegativeQuestionShort answers
I / you / we / they play
he / she / it plays		 I / you / we / they don't play
he / she / it doesn't play		 Do I / you / we / they play?
Does he / she / it play?		 Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
In the 3rd person singular (he, she, it) the verb takes -s only in the affirmative. In negatives and questions the -s goes to does: She likes pizza. → She doesn't like pizza. → Does she like pizza?

Spelling of the 3rd person

RuleExamples
most verbs: + -splay → plays · read → reads · live → lives
verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: + -esmiss → misses · wash → washes · watch → watches · fix → fixes · go → goes · do → does
consonant + -y: -y → -iesstudy → studies · carry → carries · fly → flies
vowel + -y: + -splay → plays · enjoy → enjoys · buy → buys
irregularhave → has · be → am / is / are

Use

We use the Present Simple for…Examples
habits and routinesI get up at seven every day.
permanent situationsShe lives in Braga. · He works in a shop.
facts and general truthsThe sun rises in the east. · Cats don't like water.
likes, dislikes and opinionsI love chocolate. · We hate Mondays. · I think it's great.
timetables and programmesThe film starts at 9. · School finishes at 5.

Adverbs and expressions of frequency

always (100%) · usually · often · sometimes · rarely / seldom · hardly ever · never (0%)

  • Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: I usually walk to school. · He never eats meat.
  • …but after the verb to be: She is always late. · They are never at home on Sundays.
  • Longer expressions go at the end (or beginning) of the sentence: every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year, on Mondays, at the weekend. I play football twice a week. · On Saturdays we go shopping.
  • Question: How often do you go to the cinema? – Once a month.

Time markers: every day / week / year · always, usually, often · on Mondays · in the morning · at the weekend · at night.

Verb to be is different: no do / does. I am / 'm not · you are / aren't · she is / isn't · Are you tired? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. The same happens with have got: He hasn't got a bike. · Have you got a pen?

sebenta.title: Present Continuous · Simple vs Continuous
sebenta.html:
Present Continuous

FormUseExamples
am / is / are + verb-ing
neg.: am not / isn't / aren't + -ing
quest.: Am / Is / Are + subject + -ing?
short answers: Yes, he is. / No, he isn't.		 • actions happening now, at the moment of speaking
• temporary situations (around now)
• changing situations
• future arrangements (see p. 7)		 Look! It's raining.
I'm studying for a test this week.
My English is getting better.
We're meeting Ana at six.

Time markers: now · right now · at the moment · today · this week · these days · Look! · Listen!

Spelling of -ing

  • Most verbs: + -ing: play → playing · eat → eating · study → studying
  • Verbs ending in -e: drop the e: make → making · write → writing · have → having
  • One vowel + one consonant (short, stressed): double the consonant: run → running · swim → swimming · sit → sitting · begin → beginning
  • Verbs ending in -ie: -ie → -ying: lie → lying · die → dying

Present Simple vs Present Continuous

Present SimplePresent Continuous
habits, routines, things that are generally trueactions happening now or around now, temporary
I play tennis every Saturday.I'm playing tennis at the moment.
She wears glasses.She's wearing a red dress today.
He works in a bank.He's working at home this week.
always, usually, often, every day, on Sundaysnow, at the moment, today, this week, Look!

Stative verbs (verbs not used in the continuous)

Some verbs describe states, not actions. We use them in the Present Simple, even when we talk about now:

GroupVerbsExamples
likes and dislikeslike, love, hate, prefer, want, need, wishI want an ice cream. (not I'm wanting)
thinking and opinionknow, think (= believe), believe, understand, remember, forget, meanI don't understand this exercise.
sensessee, hear, smell, taste, sound, seemThis soup tastes delicious.
possessionhave (= own), have got, own, belong, costThis bag belongs to me.
Some verbs have two meanings: I think he's nice (opinion) / I'm thinking about the test (mental activity) · She has a car (possession) / She's having lunch (action) · I see the problem (understand) / I'm seeing the doctor at 4 (meeting).

Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.

There was a party yesterday. · There were lots of people. · Was there any food? · I was born in 2013.

Other verbs

The Past Simple form is the same for all persons. After didn't and Did the verb goes back to the infinitive: She went out. → She didn't go out. → Did she go out? (not didn't went)

Spelling of -ed

RuleExamples
most verbs: + -edplay → played · watch → watched · visit → visited
verbs ending in -e: + -dlive → lived · dance → danced · like → liked
