Use

We use the Past Simple for…Examples
finished actions at a definite time in the pastWe visited London last summer.
a sequence of past actions (one after the other)She opened the door, looked inside and screamed.
past habits and statesWhen I was six, I loved cartoons.

Time markers: yesterday · last night / week / month / year · two days ago · in 2015 · when I was a child · then · the other day.

Questions with question words: Where did you go? · What did she say? · Why didn't they come? But when the question word is the subject, there is no did: Who phoned? · What happened?

sebenta.title: Past Continuous · Past Simple vs Continuous
sebenta.html:
Past Continuous

FormUseExamples
was / were + verb-ing
neg.: wasn't / weren't + -ing
quest.: Was / Were + subject + -ing?
short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren't.		 • an action in progress at a specific moment in the past
• background to a shorter action that interrupts it
• two actions in progress at the same time
• to set the scene in a story		 At 8 o'clock last night I was doing my homework.
I was walking home when I saw the accident.
While I was cooking, my brother was watching TV.
The sun was shining and the birds were singing.

Time markers: at 7 o'clock yesterday · at that moment · all day yesterday · while · when · as.

Stative verbs (know, like, want, understand, believe, belong…) are not used in the Past Continuous: I knew the answer (not I was knowing).

Past Simple vs Past Continuous

Past SimplePast Continuous
a complete, finished actionan action in progress (we don't know if it finished)
I read a book last night. (I finished it)I was reading a book at 10 pm. (in the middle of it)
a sequence of actionstwo actions happening at the same time
He came in, sat down and started to talk.He was talking while she was listening.
the short action that interruptsthe long action that is interrupted
…when the phone rang.I was sleeping when the phone rang.

When and while

PatternExamples
Past Continuous + when + Past SimpleWe were having dinner when the lights went out.
When + Past Simple, Past ContinuousWhen the lights went out, we were having dinner.
While / As + Past Continuous, Past SimpleWhile I was waiting for the bus, I met an old friend.
While + Past Continuous, Past ContinuousWhile Mum was cooking, Dad was laying the table.
when + Past Simple = the short action that interrupts · while / as + Past Continuous = the longer action in the background. When the when / while clause comes first, use a comma. Compare: When she arrived, we were having lunch (lunch had started) / When she arrived, we had lunch (first she arrived, then lunch).

Telling a story

Use the Past Continuous to describe the scene (weather, what people were doing) and the Past Simple for the events, one after the other: It was raining and I was walking home from school. Suddenly, a car stopped next to me and a man got out…

Useful words: suddenly · at that moment · then · after that · luckily · unfortunately · in the end.

sebenta.title: Used to
sebenta.html:
FormUseExamples
used to + infinitive
neg.: didn't use to + infinitive
quest.: Did + subject + use to + infinitive?
short answers: Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.		 • past habits that are no longer true
• past states and situations that have changed
• only in the past: there is no present form		 I used to play with dolls. (I don't now.)
She used to have long hair.
We didn't use to like vegetables.
Did you use to live here?
Spelling: used to in the affirmative, but use to after didn't and Did (the -d goes into did, like any other verb in the Past Simple): He didn't use to wear glasses. The form is the same for all persons: I / she / they used to.

Used to vs Past Simple

Used toPast Simple
repeated actions or states over a period in the past (not now)a single action, or an action that happened a specific number of times
I used to go to the beach every summer.I went to the beach yesterday.
She used to be very shy.She was shy at the party last night.
They used to live in Porto.They lived in Porto for two years. (with a period or number: Past Simple)
  • Used to is never used for something that happened once: I broke my leg in 2020 (not I used to break).
  • With how long, for, in + year use the Past Simple: I lived there for five years.
  • To talk about the present, use the Present Simple with now / nowadays / these days: I used to walk to school, but now I take the bus.

Talking about changes: then and now

Then (used to)Now (Present Simple)
I used to watch cartoons.Now I watch series.
My dad used to have a moustache.He doesn't have one any more.
There used to be a park here.There's a shopping centre now.
We didn't use to have a dog.We've got two dogs now!

Useful expressions: when I was little / younger · in the past · years ago · at primary school · any more / no longer · nowadays / these days.

Be careful with be used to (= be accustomed to), which you will study later: I used to get up early (a past habit, not now) is different from I'm used to getting up early (it's normal for me now). In 7.º ano you only need used to + infinitive.

Practice patterns

  • What did you use to do at the weekend when you were six? – I used to go to my grandparents' house.
  • Did you use to like school? – Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
  • People used to write letters; now they send messages.

sebenta.title: The future: will, going to, Present Continuous
sebenta.html:
Will

FormUseExamples
will ('ll) + infinitive
neg.: will not (won't) + infinitive
quest.: Will + subject + infinitive?
short answers: Yes, I will. / No, I won't.		 • predictions based on what we think or believe
• spontaneous decisions (made at the moment of speaking)
• promises, offers and requests
• facts about the future		 I think it will be a great film.
I'm thirsty. I'll have a glass of water.
I won't tell anyone, I promise. · I'll carry that for you.
She will be 13 next month.

Markers: tomorrow · next week · soon · in the future · in 2050 · I think / I hope / I'm sure / probably / maybe / perhaps.

Going to

FormUseExamples
am / is / are going to + infinitive
neg.: 'm not / isn't / aren't going to
quest.: Am / Is / Are + subject + going to + infinitive?		 • plans and intentions (decided before speaking)
• predictions based on evidence (what we can see now)		 I'm going to study medicine.
We're going to visit Rome in July.
Look at the sky! It's going to rain.
Careful! You're going to fall!

Present Continuous for the future

FormUseExamples
am / is / are + verb-ing + future time expression • fixed arrangements: the time and place are already decided, often with other people I'm meeting Rita at 5 tomorrow.
We're flying to London on Friday.
What are you doing tonight?

Will vs going to vs Present Continuous

WillGoing toPresent Continuous
decision made nowdecision made before (intention)arrangement with time / place / people
"There's no bread." "I'll go and buy some."I'm going to buy bread – it's on my list.I'm having lunch with Tom at 1.
prediction: opinionprediction: evidence—
I think Porto will win.It's 3–0. Porto is going to win.
Typical mistakes: I will to go → I will go · She wills → She will · I'm going to London tomorrow is correct (arrangement), but I going to → I'm going to · Will you to help me? → Will you help me?

Time clauses: after when, as soon as, before, after, until, if we use the Present Simple, not will: I'll call you when I get home. · If it rains, we'll stay in.

Useful phrases: What are you going to do in the summer? · What are your plans for the weekend? · I'm not sure, but I'll probably … · Maybe I'll … · I'd like to … · I hope to …

Making questions

Yes / No question with other verbsDo / Does / Did + subject + infinitive?Do you like rap? · Did he call?

Question words: what · who · where · when · why · how · which · whose · how many / how much · how often · how long · how old · what time · what kind of.

Short answers

Answer with Yes / No + subject pronoun + auxiliary. Never repeat the main verb, and don't contract affirmative answers.

QuestionYesNo
Are you hungry?Yes, I am. (not Yes, I'm)No, I'm not.
Does she play the guitar?Yes, she does.No, she doesn't.
Did they win?Yes, they did.No, they didn't.
Was it expensive?Yes, it was.No, it wasn't.
Is he sleeping?Yes, he is.No, he isn't.

Auxiliary verbs (do, does, did, am, is, are, was, were, will, can, have got) are the key to negatives, questions and short answers. Find the auxiliary first; if there isn't one, add do / does / did.

sebenta.title: Comparatives, superlatives and as … as
sebenta.html:
AdjectiveComparative (+ than)Superlative (the …)
one syllable: tall, cheap, fasttaller, cheaper, fasterthe tallest, the cheapest, the fastest
ending in -e: nice, large, safenicer, larger, saferthe nicest, the largest, the safest
one vowel + one consonant: big, hot, thinbigger, hotter, thinnerthe biggest, the hottest, the thinnest
two syllables ending in -y: happy, funny, easyhappier, funnier, easierthe happiest, the funniest, the easiest
two or more syllables: modern, famous, expensive, intelligentmore modern, more famous, more expensivethe most modern, the most famous, the most expensive
irregular: good, bad, far, little, much / manybetter, worse, farther / further, less, morethe best, the worst, the farthest / furthest, the least, the most

Some two-syllable adjectives take either form: clever, quiet, simple, narrow → cleverer / more clever. Adjectives ending in -ful, -less, -ing, -ed always take more / most: more careful, the most boring, more tired.

Comparatives

  • comparative + than: Lisbon is bigger than Faro. · Maths is more difficult than History.
  • With pronouns after than, use the object form: She's taller than me / than him.
  • less + adjective + than (the opposite of more): The bus is less expensive than the train.
  • Modifiers: much / a lot / far + comparative (big difference), a bit / a little / slightly + comparative (small difference): It's much colder today. · He's a bit older than me.
  • comparative and comparative = a continuing change: The days are getting longer and longer. · It's more and more popular.

Superlatives

  • the + superlative + in (places, groups) / of (periods): the tallest boy in the class · the best day of the year · the most famous singer in the world
  • Often with ever: It's the best film I've ever seen. · He's the funniest person I know.
  • one of the + superlative + plural noun: She's one of the best players in the team.
  • by far + superlative: It's by far the most expensive phone.

(Not) as … as

StructureMeaningExamples
as + adjective + asthe sameRui is as tall as his dad. · This test was as easy as the last one.
not as / so + adjective + asless thanPorto isn't as big as Lisbon. (= Lisbon is bigger)
twice / three times as + adjective + asmultiplyingMy bag is twice as heavy as yours.
the same (+ noun) as · different fromequal / not equalHer phone is the same as mine. · He's different from his brother.
Typical mistakes: more bigger → bigger · the most easiest → the easiest · more good → better · bigger that → bigger than · the taller in the class → the tallest in the class · as tall than → as tall as.

sebenta.title: Quantifiers
sebenta.html:
Countable nouns have a plural (an apple, two apples); uncountable nouns have no plural and no a / an (water, bread, money, homework, information, advice): a glass of water, a piece of advice.

QuantifierCountableUncountableUsed in…Examples
some✓ plural✓affirmatives; offers and requestsI've got some apples. · Would you like some tea?
any✓ plural✓negatives and questionsWe haven't got any milk. · Are there any eggs?
a lot of / lots of✓✓large quantity, all sentence typesShe eats a lot of fruit. · There are lots of people.
many✓ plural✗mainly negatives and questionsThere aren't many shops. · How many brothers have you got?
much✗✓mainly negatives and questionsI don't have much money. · How much sugar do you want?
a few✓ plural✗a small number (positive idea)I've got a few friends in London.
a little✗✓a small amount (positive idea)There's a little milk left.
too many / too much✓ plural / ✗✗ / ✓more than necessary (a problem)Too many cars. · Too much noise.
enough✓✓the necessary quantityWe have enough chairs. · Is there enough food?

Too and enough

too + adjective / adverb (= more than is good): This coffee is too hot. · He drives too fast. · adjective + enough (= as much as necessary): The water is warm enough. · You're not old enough to drive. · enough + noun: I haven't got enough money.

too is negative (a problem) – very is only intensity: The bag is very heavy, but I can carry it. / The bag is too heavy – I can't carry it. Enough goes after adjectives but before nouns.

+Adverbs of manner

Adjectives describe nouns (a slow car); adverbs of manner describe how an action is done and usually go after the verb or the object (He drives slowly).

RuleExamples
adjective + -lyquick → quickly · careful → carefully · quiet → quietly · bad → badly
-y → -ily · -le → -ly · -ic → -allyhappy → happily · easy → easily · terrible → terribly · fantastic → fantastically
irregulargood → well · fast → fast · hard → hard · late → late · early → early

She is a good singer. → She sings well. · He's a careful driver. → He drives carefully.

sebenta.title: Modal verbs: can, could, should, must, have to
sebenta.html:
Modal verbs are followed by the infinitive without to, have no -s in the 3rd person and make negatives and questions without do: She can swim. · He mustn't run. · Should I go? · Yes, you should. Have to behaves like a normal verb: she has to, she doesn't have to, Does she have to…?

ModalUseExamples
can
neg.: can't / cannot		ability (present)I can play the piano. · She can't drive.
permission (informal)Can I go to the toilet? · You can't use your phone in class.
requests and offersCan you help me? · Can I carry that for you?
could
neg.: couldn't		ability in the pastI could read when I was four. · He couldn't come yesterday.
polite requests (more polite than can)Could you open the window, please?
possibility / suggestionWe could go to the cinema. · It could be true.
should
neg.: shouldn't		advice (it's a good idea)You should see a doctor. · You shouldn't eat so many sweets.
asking for adviceShould I tell her? · What should I do?
must
neg.: mustn't		obligation (the speaker thinks it is necessary); rulesI must finish this today. · Students must wear a uniform.
mustn't = prohibition (it's not allowed)You mustn't smoke here. · You mustn't be late.
have to
neg.: don't have to		obligation (a rule or an external necessity)I have to be home by 10. · She has to wear glasses.
don't have to = no obligation (it isn't necessary)You don't have to come if you're tired. · He doesn't have to work on Fridays.
mustn't ≠ don't have to: You mustn't touch that! (it's forbidden) / You don't have to wash up – I'll do it. (it isn't necessary). In the affirmative, must and have to are very similar; must is more personal, have to is about rules.

PresentPastFuture

Yesterday I had to stay at school until 6. · Next year you'll have to study harder. · When I was five I couldn't ride a bike; now I can.

Typical mistakes: She cans → She can · I can to swim → I can swim · Do you can…? → Can you…? · He must to go → He must go · I don't must → I mustn't / I don't have to · She have to → She has to.

sebenta.title: Indefinite pronouns
sebenta.html:
Indefinite pronouns talk about people, things and places without saying exactly who, what or where. They are formed with some-, any-, no-, every- + -body / -one (people), -thing (things) and -where (places).

PeopleThingsPlacesUsed in…
some-somebody / someonesomethingsomewhereaffirmative sentences; offers, requests
any-anybody / anyoneanythinganywherenegative sentences and questions
no-nobody / no onenothingnowhereaffirmative verb, negative meaning
every-everybody / everyoneeverythingeverywhereall sentence types (= all)

Use

RuleExamples
some- in affirmative sentencesSomebody is knocking at the door. · I want to go somewhere hot. · There's something in my eye.
some- in offers and requests (we expect "yes")Would you like something to drink? · Can someone help me, please?
any- in questionsIs there anything to eat? · Did anyone call? · Are you going anywhere this summer?
any- in negative sentences (with not)I didn't see anybody. · She doesn't want anything. · We didn't go anywhere.
any- = "it doesn't matter which" (affirmative)You can sit anywhere. · Anyone can learn to cook.
no- with an affirmative verb (one negative only)Nobody came. · There's nothing in the fridge. · We went nowhere.
every- = all the people / things / placesEverybody likes her. · I've told you everything. · I looked everywhere for my keys.
One negative only! I didn't see nobody → I didn't see anybody / I saw nobody. · There isn't nothing → There isn't anything / There's nothing.

Grammar notes

  • Indefinite pronouns are singular: the verb takes -s / is / was: Everybody is here. · Nothing happens in this town. · Someone has taken my pen.
  • But we refer back to them with they / their: If anyone calls, tell them I'm out. · Everybody brought their books.
  • Adjectives go after the pronoun: something interesting · somewhere quiet · nobody famous
  • else = other / different: Would you like anything else? · Somebody else can do it. · Let's go somewhere else.

With nouns: some + plural / uncountable (I need some shoes), any in negatives and questions (Have you got any brothers?), no + noun (I have no idea), every + singular (Every student has a locker). Somebody = someone (-body is more informal).

sebenta.title: Sequence connectors · Other connectors
sebenta.html:
Sequence connectors (ordering events and instructions)

PositionConnectorsExamples
beginningFirst, Firstly, First of all, To begin with, At first (= in the beginning, before a change)First, mix the flour and the eggs.
At first I didn't like him, but now we're friends.
middleThen, Next, After that, Afterwards, Secondly, Later, Meanwhile (= at the same time), SuddenlyThen add the milk. After that, bake it for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, prepare the sauce.
endFinally, In the end, At last (after waiting a long time), Eventually (after a long time / problems), LastlyFinally, serve with ice cream.
In the end, we decided to stay at home.

Sequence connectors usually go at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma. They are used in recipes, instructions, stories and narratives (with the Past Simple) and in describing routines (with the Present Simple).

Time connectors inside the sentence: when, while, as soon as, before, after, until: Before you go out, close the windows. · I'll text you as soon as I arrive. · Wait here until I come back. With before / after you can also use -ing: After finishing my homework, I went out.

Other useful connectors

FunctionConnectorsExamples
Additionand · also (before the main verb) · too / as well (end) · both … andI like tennis and football. · I also like golf. · My sister plays too.
Contrastbut · however (start of sentence, + comma) · although / even though + clauseIt was raining, but we went out. · It was raining. However, we went out. · Although it was raining, we went out.
Reasonbecause + subject + verb · because of + noun · as / sinceI stayed in because I was tired. · The match was cancelled because of the rain.
Resultso · that's why · so + adjective + thatI was tired, so I went to bed. · It was so cold that we stayed in.
Purposeto + infinitive · in order to · for + noun / -ingI went to the shop to buy milk. · This app is for learning English.
Alternativeor · either … or · neither … norTea or coffee? · You can either walk or take the bus.
Examplefor example · for instance · such as · likeI love sports such as swimming and cycling.
Opinion / conclusionIn my opinion · I think (that) · To sum up · All in allIn my opinion, school uniforms are a good idea.
because + clause (subject + verb) / because of + noun: because it rained / because of the rain. although + clause: no but in the same sentence (Although it rained, but we went out). However starts a new sentence and takes a comma.

Model: describing a routine / a recipe / a story

First, I get up at 7 and have a shower. Then I have breakfast. After that, I walk to school because it's near my house. In the afternoon I do my homework and I play basketball. Finally, I have dinner with my family and I go to bed at about 10.

Useful phrases for writing

PurposePhrases
Describing a personHe / She is tall and slim, with short curly hair and brown eyes. · She's got freckles / glasses. · He's in his thirties. · She looks friendly.
PersonalityHe's funny, kind and hard-working, but sometimes a bit lazy / shy / moody. · She's very outgoing and easy to get on with. · What I like most about him is …
Feelings and relationshipsI get on well with … · We have a lot in common. · She makes me laugh. · I feel nervous / excited / bored when … · We've been friends since …
Giving opinionsI think (that) … · In my opinion, … · I (don't) agree with … · I prefer … to … · I'd rather … · My favourite … is … because … · It's great / boring / delicious / too expensive.
Food, shopping, entertainmentI'm into … · I can't stand … · It's worth watching / buying. · It's good value for money. · The film is about … · The best thing about it is …
Informal email / letterHi Ana, / Dear Tom, · Thanks for your email. · How are you? · I'm writing to tell you about … · Guess what! · Anyway, I have to go now. · Write back soon! · Love, / Take care, / See you soon, / Best wishes,
Telling a storyLast summer, … · One day, … · Suddenly, … · Luckily, … · Unfortunately, … · In the end, … · It was the best / worst day of my life.
Punctuation reminder: capital letters for I, names, days, months, nationalities and languages (Monday, July, Portuguese); a comma after connectors at the start of a sentence (However, … / First, …); a question mark after questions; apostrophes in contractions (don't, I'm, she's) and possessives (Ana's bag).
